svg.text: The first law of thermodynamics, isothermal and adiabatic processes, reversibility
Q = (U2 - U1) + W -> Q = delta U + W (6.5)

g.text: heat Q added to a system appears as an increase delta U in
its internal energy plus the work W it does on its surroundings;
delta U = Q - W is the same for every process between two states
1 conservation principle: energy changes form (chemical to thermal)
but the total in an isolated system stays constant
2 wider applicability: chemical reactions, electrical systems, nuclear
reactions, all forms of energy and all processes
bicycle pump (Fig. 6.6): pushing the piston
rapidly does work on the air; its internal
energy and temperature rise (the thermometer
shows it); no time for heat to escape
human metabolism: walking, running, growing
cells need energy; delta U = Q - W applied to
the body shows that work lowers its internal
energy, which the food we eat restores
isothermal: delta U = 0, Q = W; slow, P1 V1 = P2 V2
adiabatic: Q = 0, W = -delta U; rapid; P V^gamma = const

svg.text: Isothermal and adiabatic processes; reversible and irreversible processes (6.5)

g.text: isothermal: constant temperature, so Boyle's law applies and PV stays constant; an ideal gas's internal energy depends only on T, so delta U = 0
and Q = W: the heat supplied equals the external work; heat transfer takes time, so the change must be slow; the P-V curve is an isotherm
adiabatic: no heat enters or leaves, Q = 0, so W = -delta U: expansion does work at the expense of internal energy and T falls, compression raises T;
happens when the gas expands or is compressed rapidly or in an insulated cylinder: a burst tyre, air in a sound wave, cloud formation;
P V^gamma = constant, gamma = molar specific heat at constant pressure over that at constant volume; the curve is an adiabat, steeper than the isotherm
reversible: can be retraced in exactly reverse order without any change in the surroundings; heat absorbed is given back, work done by is done on; the
substance returns to its original condition; no actual change is completely reversible, but slow liquefaction, evaporation and slow compression of a gas nearly are
cycle: a succession of events that brings the system back to its initial condition; a reversible cycle is one in which all the changes are reversible
irreversible: cannot be retraced by reversing the controlling factors; all sudden changes and those involving friction or dissipation by conduction,
convection or radiation; an explosion is highly irreversible
Brain Teaser: why does the internal energy of an ideal gas stay constant in an isothermal expansion? Because U depends on T alone, and T does not change
